pages.x: In the early 2000s American lenders gave home loans to millions of people who could not really afford them, often with low payments at first that jumped later. Banks bundled thousands of these mortgages together and sold them around the world as safe investments. As long as house prices kept rising, everyone seemed to win.

In 2006 American house prices began to fall. Millions of borrowers could not keep up their payments, and the bundles of loans turned out to be worth far less than anyone had thought. No one knew which banks held the bad debts, so banks stopped lending to each other. In Britain savers queued in the street to take their money out of Northern Rock.

On 15 September 2008 Lehman Brothers, a bank founded 158 years before, went bust, the largest bankruptcy in American history. Panic swept the world's markets. The next day the government took over AIG, a giant insurer, to stop it collapsing too, and for a few weeks it seemed that the whole banking system might fail.

Governments poured hundreds of billions into their banks to keep them alive, and central banks cut interest rates almost to zero and created new money. In Iceland all three big banks collapsed within days, and the króna lost half its value. People were furious that bankers were rescued while ordinary people paid.

The world fell into its deepest slump since the 1930s. World trade shrank, factories closed, and in the United States millions of families lost their homes. In Spain and Greece more than half of all young people looking for work could not find it.

The crisis spread to European countries with big debts. Greece, which had understated how much it owed, had to be rescued three times by the other euro countries, in return for deep cuts that shrank its economy by a quarter. Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus needed help too.

The crisis left a deep anger at bankers who were bailed out while others lost their jobs and homes. It fed protests such as Occupy Wall Street, and helped the rise of angry new parties on the left and the right. Banks now have to keep bigger cushions of money, in case another crash comes.
